 has completed a multibillion-dollar all-cash acquisition of a biotechnology name focused on next-generation antibody therapies, marking the company's largest transaction in several years and underscoring how aggressively large drugmakers continue to pursue dealmaking to refill pipelines ahead of looming patent expirations. The North Chicago-based healthcare company, whose portfolio spans immunology, oncology, aesthetics, and neuroscience, has leaned heavily on dealmaking in recent years to offset an anticipated slowdown tied to biosimilar competition against its former flagship immunology medicine. The newly absorbed business brings a late-stage, half-life-extended antibody candidate targeting a key inflammatory pathway implicated in atopic dermatitis, along with an earlier-stage pipeline of antibody combinations aimed at asthma. Under the terms of the now-completed transaction, stockholders of the acquired company received an all-cash payout, with the deal expected to modestly weigh on near-term earnings before turning additive in the years ahead as the newly acquired pipeline matures toward commercialization. The rationale behind the transaction centers on deepening AbbVie's presence in immunology well beyond its two current flagship medicines, both of which face their own eventual exclusivity challenges even as they continue to drive substantial growth today. Management has been explicit that dealmaking remains a central pillar of the broader strategy to manage the transition away from reliance on a shrinking legacy immunology franchise, with the newly acquired antibody pipeline offering a next-generation mechanism distinct from the company's existing immunology medicines. That distinction matters because it broadens the mechanistic diversity of the overall immunology portfolio rather than simply adding another medicine competing through the same biological pathway. Executives have framed the acquisition as consistent with a broader pattern of steady, disciplined dealmaking rather than a single transformative bet, reflecting a philosophy of continuously refreshing the pipeline through a mix of smaller and occasionally larger transactions rather than relying on any single blockbuster to sustain growth indefinitely. The backdrop against which this transaction unfolds remains the ongoing erosion of the company's former flagship immunology medicine, which has faced accelerating biosimilar competition following the loss of patent protection. Management has repeatedly pointed to the two newer immunology medicines that have effectively replaced the legacy franchise as evidence that the broader transition has proceeded roughly as planned, with combined growth from those two medicines largely offsetting the ongoing decline from biosimilar erosion. Even so, both newer medicines will eventually face their own patent expirations, reinforcing why continued dealmaking to diversify the immunology pipeline beyond those two products remains a persistent management priority. The newly acquired antibody pipeline, targeting different inflammatory pathways than either of the two current flagship medicines, gives the company a further layer of diversification within immunology, reducing the degree to which any single mechanism or medicine can single-handedly determine the trajectory of the broader immunology business. Attention now turns to an upcoming appearance by senior management at a major healthcare-focused gathering hosted by a prominent Wall Street bank, where commentary on the newly completed acquisition, integration plans, and broader capital allocation priorities will likely draw close attention. These kinds of appearances typically give management a platform to expand on themes raised in scheduled disclosures, including how quickly the newly acquired antibody programs could advance toward late-stage readouts and how integration is proceeding operationally. With the stock already carrying elevated attention following the deal's completion, the conference appearance adds an extra layer of scrutiny, since any additional detail on program timelines or integration costs could meaningfully shape how the market prices the longer-term case for the expanded immunology pipeline. Beyond immunology, the oncology and aesthetics businesses continue to contribute meaningfully to overall growth, giving the company additional avenues for expansion beyond its heavy reliance on immunology medicines. The oncology portfolio spans blood cancer and solid tumor treatments, with several newer therapies continuing to gain traction as older medicines face growing competitive pressure. The aesthetics business, encompassing well-known facial injectable and body-contouring brands, has faced a somewhat uneven stretch recently as discretionary consumer spending on elective cosmetic procedures softened in certain markets, though management continues to view the category as an important long-term growth contributor once broader consumer spending patterns stabilize. Together, these businesses provide a diversification benefit that reduces the company's overall dependence on immunology alone sustaining growth indefinitely, an increasingly important consideration given the intensifying competitive pressure facing the legacy immunology franchise. The broader healthcare group has softened this week alongside financial names as a hotter than expected jobs report revived expectations that the Federal Reserve could keep its stance firmer for longer, pushing Treasury yields higher and prompting a rotation away from some defensive corners of the market. AbbVie has traded broadly in line with that softer tone across healthcare names generally, even as the newly completed acquisition and conference appearance have kept the stock in sharp focus relative to quieter peers. Higher yields tend to weigh more heavily on slower-growing, distribution-paying businesses since they raise the bar for how attractive a steady payout looks relative to safer alternatives, a dynamic that has periodically pressured healthcare names even when company-specific developments have been constructive. Competition across inflammatory disease treatment, spanning conditions such as atopic dermatitis, asthma, and related autoimmune disorders, continues to intensify as multiple large drugmakers pursue next-generation antibody mechanisms aimed at capturing share from older, less targeted therapies. The newly acquired antibody pipeline enters a field already populated by several established and emerging rivals, each pursuing differentiated mechanisms aimed at improving efficacy, dosing convenience, or safety relative to existing standard treatments. Differentiation within this crowded field will likely hinge on late-stage clinical results that have not yet fully matured, meaning the ultimate commercial success of the newly acquired pipeline remains dependent on further clinical execution rather than already-established data. That competitive intensity underscores why continuous pipeline funding, rather than reliance on any single medicine, has become the dominant strategy among large immunology-focused drugmakers navigating an increasingly crowded therapeutic landscape. Funding the newly completed acquisition required a combination of cash on hand and additional debt issuance, a trade-off management has defended as consistent with the company's broader disciplined dealmaking approach even as it modestly increases near-term leverage. Executives have continued to prioritize debt reduction alongside steady dividend growth and selective additional dealmaking, a balance that has become increasingly important as the company absorbs a steady stream of transactions aimed at diversifying its pipeline. The company's strong underlying cash generation, driven primarily by its two current flagship immunology medicines alongside a growing oncology contribution, continues to provide the financial flexibility needed to fund debt reduction, dividend growth, and further dealmaking simultaneously without forcing difficult trade-offs between these competing capital allocation priorities. Even as the newly completed acquisition is expected to modestly weigh on near-term earnings, management has continued to express confidence in the broader guidance framework for the current period, reflecting continued strength across the two current flagship immunology medicines and the growing oncology contribution. That confidence, delivered alongside the deal's completion, indicates management views the near-term earnings impact from the acquisition as a worthwhile trade-off for the longer-term diversification benefit the newly acquired pipeline provides. Guidance commentary has emphasized that underlying operating trends across the existing portfolio remain solid, with the acquisition-related earnings impact treated as a discrete, well-understood item rather than a sign of broader operating softness across the base business. Within the broader market backdrop, defensive healthcare names like AbbVie have offered a mixed signal this week, with the sector's overall softness partly offsetting company-specific developments tied to the newly completed acquisition. When broad gauges such as S&P 500 swing on macro headlines tied to shifting rate expectations, healthcare names carrying steady but slower-growing distributions tend to see somewhat muted relative performance compared with higher-momentum corners of the market such as technology and industrial names. That dynamic has played out again this week, with megacap technology names among the session's laggards even as select industrial names posted gains, leaving healthcare broadly, and AbbVie specifically, caught in the middle of a market still working through uneven signals on the path for interest rates. With the transaction now closed, integration priorities center on retaining key research talent from the acquired organization, aligning clinical development timelines with the broader immunology pipeline, and beginning the process of advancing the newly absorbed programs through remaining stages of testing. Management has emphasized a light-touch integration approach designed to preserve the acquired team's research culture and momentum rather than immediately folding operations into existing structures, a strategy that has become increasingly common among large drugmakers acquiring smaller, science-driven biotechnology names. How smoothly that integration proceeds over the coming months will likely factor heavily into market participants' broader assessment of whether the transaction ultimately proves additive to the company's long-term immunology positioning. Beyond immunology, oncology, and aesthetics, the neuroscience business has continued to expand its footprint across migraine treatment, psychiatric conditions, and movement disorders, providing yet another avenue for growth that further diversifies the company away from reliance on immunology alone. Recent launches within the neuroscience portfolio have gained steady traction with prescribers, aided by a commercial infrastructure built up over years of experience marketing complex, chronic-condition treatments to specialist physicians. Management has continued to highlight neuroscience as an underappreciated piece of the broader growth story, noting that while the segment remains smaller than immunology or oncology in absolute terms, its growth trajectory has been consistently strong and increasingly meaningful to overall results. The segment benefits from many of the same commercial capabilities the company has honed within immunology, including established relationships with specialist prescribers and a track record of navigating complex reimbursement environments for chronic, high-cost treatments. That transferable commercial expertise has allowed the neuroscience business to scale more efficiently than might otherwise be expected for a relatively newer growth area, reducing the incremental spending required to support continued expansion. As the newly acquired immunology pipeline works through remaining stages of testing over the coming years, management has signaled that neuroscience, alongside oncology, will likely take on growing importance as a further hedge against the eventual decline of the legacy immunology medicine, giving the company multiple simultaneous growth engines rather than relying on a single business line to carry overall performance. That multi-pronged approach, spanning immunology, oncology, neuroscience, and aesthetics, continues to underpin management's broader case that the company is well positioned to manage its various patent-related transitions without a prolonged period of stagnant overall growth. Continued spending on late-stage neuroscience programs, alongside the newly absorbed immunology pipeline, reflects a broader willingness to fund multiple parallel research efforts rather than concentrating capital in a single therapeutic area, a strategy that has become increasingly common among large, diversified healthcare companies seeking to manage several simultaneous patent transitions across different parts of their business at once. Talent retention within the newly absorbed research organization has also emerged as an early integration priority, with management emphasizing continuity of the acquired scientific teams as a way of preserving the institutional knowledge behind the late-stage antibody programs now folded into the broader immunology pipeline. The aesthetics business, while facing a softer near-term stretch tied to discretionary consumer spending pressure on elective cosmetic procedures, continues to maintain a leading position across facial injectable and body-contouring categories that management views as durable over a longer horizon. Consumer willingness to spend on elective aesthetic procedures tends to track broader confidence in discretionary spending capacity, making the category more sensitive to shifting economic conditions than the company's core immunology and oncology businesses. Even so, management has continued allocating capital in expanding the aesthetics portfolio through new product introductions and broader geographic reach, betting that longer-term demand for these categories remains structurally intact even through periods of softer near-term spending. That patient approach to a cyclically sensitive business reflects a broader philosophy of maintaining leading category positions through temporary softness rather than retreating, positioning the aesthetics unit to capture a disproportionate share of any eventual rebound in discretionary spending on elective procedures once broader consumer conditions stabilize. title: Is AbbVie Stock Too Reliant On Skyrizi? - Trefis
content: AbbVie (ABBV) trades at $256.46, roughly 96% of its 52-week high, after returning 24.1% over the past twelve months against 19.7% for the S&P 500. That price buys a business where about a third of guided 2026 revenue comes from one drug. The market reads that concentration as strength. It is worth reading it the other way too. SKYRIZI, AbbVie’s psoriasis and Crohn’s disease biologic, sold $5.5 billion in Q2 2026, up 24% on an operational basis, inside total net revenues of nearly $17 billion that grew 10.2% as reported. Management’s full-year 2026 forecast puts SKYRIZI at about $21.7 billion against roughly $67.6 billion of total net revenues. That is 32% of AbbVie in one molecule. The franchise earns its reputation. In psoriasis, management says SKYRIZI leads market share in more than 30 countries and takes new and switching patients at four times the rate of any other biologic or oral treatment in the US. That strength is what makes the number uncomfortable. The company already ran this experiment. HUMIRA global sales were $756 million in Q2 2026, down 36.1% on an operational basis, which management attributes to biosimilar competition and calls in line with expectations. SKYRIZI now sells over seven times what HUMIRA does in a quarter. The calm language is the point. An exclusivity loss is not a stumble management can fix. It arrives on a schedule, and SKYRIZI’s patents already have a date on them. Management says SKYRIZI’s composition of matter patent runs to 2033, later US patents, granted and still in process, extend into the mid-2030s, and regulatory data protection holds until 2031. It also says it has seen no degradation in prescription trends since a competing oral treatment launched earlier in 2026. These expectations reflect management’s current internal tracking and forward-looking guidance. The investigational assets and label expansions meant to broaden AbbVie’s post-2030 base have yet to reach the market. Sixteen-week readouts for lutikizumab and RINVOQ in hidradenitis suppurativa are due before the end of 2026. A Phase 2b trial combining SKYRIZI with a novel antibody in Crohn’s disease and ulcerative colitis is only in start-up. The Apogee Therapeutics deal, which adds dermatology and respiratory assets, was, as of the Q2 2026 earnings call, expected to close in Q3 2026, and its $0.14 of anticipated dilution more than offsets the $0.10 AbbVie added to its full-year 2026 adjusted earnings outlook. The one launch that is close makes the problem worse. A US decision on SKYRIZI subcutaneous induction in Crohn’s disease is due in the fall of 2026, a European application was submitted in August 2026, and management expects a meaningful acceleration for SKYRIZI from it, though the company says that will probably start showing early in 2027. Every win here deepens the same dependency. So how worried should you be? Worried enough to size the position on purpose. AbbVie’s largest product continues to outpace the overall business while the pipeline meant to diversify it is still generating zero revenue, and options markets are pricing business as usual: implied volatility sits at 25, the 44th percentile of its trailing one-year range, reflecting an ordinary volatility environment rather than any elevated expectation of near-term turbulence. Watch whether RINVOQ, the neuroscience portfolio and the Apogee assets grow the non-SKYRIZI base faster than SKYRIZI grows. You cannot, and owning more of a good stock does not fix it. title: Therapeutics Stocks Q2 Recap: Benchmarking Myriad Genetics (NASDAQ:MYGN) - TradingView
content: Wrapping up Q2 earnings, we look at the numbers and key takeaways for the therapeutics stocks, including Myriad Genetics MYGN and its peers. Over the next few years, therapeutic companies, which develop a wide variety of treatments for diseases and disorders, face strong tailwinds from advancements in precision medicine (including the use of AI to improve hit rates) and growing demand for treatments targeting rare diseases. However, headwinds such as rising scrutiny over drug pricing, regulatory unknowns, and competition from larger, more resourced pharmaceutical companies could weigh on growth. The 11 therapeutics stocks we track reported a very strong Q2. As a group, revenues beat analysts’ consensus estimates by 8%. Luckily, therapeutics stocks have performed well with share prices up 19.4% on average since the latest earnings results. Founded in 1991 as one of the pioneers in translating genetic discoveries into clinical applications, Myriad Genetics MYGN develops genetic tests that assess disease risk, guide treatment decisions, and provide insights across oncology, women's health, and mental health. Myriad Genetics reported revenues of $190.7 million, down 10.5% year on year. This print fell short of analysts’ expectations by 8.2%. Overall, it was a disappointing quarter for the company with full-year revenue guidance missing analysts’ expectations significantly and a significant miss of analysts’ EPS estimates. “In the second quarter, we continued to make meaningful progress on the Cancer Care Continuum on a number of fronts, including 6% year-over-year volume growth supported by the ramp up of our expanded sales team, the launch of Prolaris + AI, the expansion of Precise MRD to include colorectal cancer (CRC) and renal cancers, along with the submission of Precise MRD breast to MolDX,” said Sam Raha, President and CEO, Myriad Genetics. Myriad Genetics delivered the weakest performance against analyst estimates and weakest full-year guidance update of the whole group. The market seems disappointed with the results as the stock is down 40.8% since reporting and currently trades at $3.18. Read our full report on Myriad Genetics here, it’s free. Founded in 1978 and pioneering treatments for some of medicine's most complex challenges, Biogen BIIB develops and markets therapies for neurological conditions, including multiple sclerosis, Alzheimer's disease, spinal muscular atrophy, and rare diseases. Biogen reported revenues of $2.74 billion, up 3.4% year on year, outperforming analysts’ expectations by 12.1%. The business had an incredible quarter with a beat of analysts’ EPS estimates and an impressive beat of analysts’ full-year EPS guidance estimates. The market seems happy with the results as the stock is up 7.5% since reporting. It currently trades at $220.99. Born from a 2013 spinoff of Abbott Laboratories' pharmaceutical business, AbbVie ABBV is a biopharmaceutical company that develops and markets medications for autoimmune diseases, cancer, neurological disorders, and other complex health conditions. AbbVie reported revenues of $16.99 billion, up 10.2% year on year, exceeding analysts’ expectations by 1.2%. Still, it was a mixed quarter as it posted a slight miss of analysts’ full-year EPS guidance estimates. Interestingly, the stock is up 1.3% since the results and currently trades at $260.72. Founded in 1989 with a mission to create medicines that treat the underlying causes of disease rather than just symptoms, Vertex Pharmaceuticals VRTX develops and markets transformative medicines for serious diseases, with a focus on cystic fibrosis, sickle cell disease, and pain management. Vertex Pharmaceuticals reported revenues of $3.33 billion, up 12.5% year on year. This print beat analysts’ expectations by 4.6%. Overall, it was a strong quarter as it also put up full-year revenue guidance slightly topping analysts’ expectations. The stock is up 15.8% since reporting and currently trades at $545. United Therapeutics reported revenues of $783.3 million, down 1.9% year on year. This number surpassed analysts’ expectations by 2.3%. title: Moderna Just Doubled Overnight, and 2 More Healthcare Stocks Could Follow It - MarketBeat
content:
Drug pricing is back on the front page, and healthcare investors have barely flinched. The White House's latest round of most-favored-nation pricing agreements brought nine more manufacturers into the fold, pushing the total to 26 companies covering 89% of the branded drug market. The sector kept climbing anyway. That gap between headline risk and price action is worth sitting with. Attention has been locked on AI and semiconductors all year, and meanwhile, healthcare and biotech have produced some of the largest single-name moves on the board. Marc Lichtenfeld of the Oxford Club sorts the opportunity by patience: one name for traders, one for the next 12 months, one to hold for a decade. Lichtenfeld's structural argument starts with the bond market. Healthcare is close to interest rate neutral, and the logic is blunt: if the 10-year yield runs to 5% or 6%, people don't stop taking their medicine. Balance sheets help too. Most biotechs aren't loaded with debt, because pre-revenue companies can't borrow against revenue they don't have. They raise capital by selling equity or converts instead. That makes the sector a rare place where a hawkish surprise doesn't reprice the whole group. Moderna NASDAQ: MRNA and Merck NYSE: MRK reported that their Phase 3 INTerpath-001 trial of intismeran autogene plus Keytruda met its primary endpoint of recurrence-free survival in patients with completely resected stage IIB–IV melanoma. It was the first positive Phase 3 for an mRNA-based cancer therapy. Moderna closed up 177% at $174.38 the day it landed. The earlier Phase 2b work reduced the risk of recurrence or death by 49% versus Keytruda alone. Full Phase 3 numbers haven't been released yet. Shares cooled after the company priced $2.6 billion in convertible notes, and Lichtenfeld reads the consolidation as a bull flag. His timeline is deliberately tight. On a daily chart, he wants confirmation inside a week or two; if the move doesn't materialize, the trade gets abandoned rather than nursed. Elevated short interest is the accelerant he's watching, since forced covering can compound a breakout. For anyone drawn to the long-term story, his suggestion is a starter position rather than a full one. Biotech stocks can sell off on good news when the good news is already expected. Pharvaris NASDAQ: PHVS is the name most investors haven't heard of. The roughly $2.4 billion company expects topline CHAPTER-3 data in the third quarter for deucrictibant, an oral therapy for hereditary angioedema, a rare and potentially life-threatening swelling disorder. Convenience is the wedge. Earlier trial work showed attack reductions in the mid-80% range, against roughly 44% for the approved oral prophylactic. An oral option that competes with injectables on efficacy is a real adherence advantage. The M&A backdrop adds a second layer. Chiesi agreed to buy KalVista Pharmaceuticals at $27 a share, about a 40% premium to the prior close, and BioCryst Pharmaceuticals NASDAQ: BCRX acquired Astria Therapeutics in a deal valued near $700 million. Lichtenfeld doesn't buy for takeouts, but he notes the space has a buyer pool. On strong data, he sees $50 as a floor case over the next year. On weak data, the stock falls hard. AbbVie NYSE: ABBV is the long hold, and Lichtenfeld's favorite healthcare name for income. Spun out of Abbott Laboratories NYSE: ABT in 2013, it has raised its dividend every year since, currently $1.73 per quarter for a yield near 2.7%. The bear case was always Humira's patent cliff. Instead, dividend growth kept compounding while the pipeline did the heavy lifting. Skyrizi cleared $5.5 billion in the second quarter, up 24%, and Rinvoq added $2.5 billion, up 25%, as Humira fell to $756 million. Management raised full-year revenue guidance to $67.6 billion. Technically, shares recently punched through the $240 area that had rejected them repeatedly. Names like this are the core of what Lichtenfeld builds portfolios around, and readers who want his monthly income picks can find them in his Oxford Income Letter dividend research. Position sizing is the discipline that separates these three. Large-cap pharma like AbbVie or Eli Lilly NYSE: LLY can absorb a failed trial. A small or mid-cap with one lead asset can be cut in half overnight. Watch the calendars, not the narratives. Moderna's follow-through window is measured in days, Pharvaris hinges on a readout due within weeks, and AbbVie asks only that you sit still. Before you consider Moderna, you'll want to hear this.
